title: The Benefit & Your Role
summary: What the Medicaid meal benefit is, what you may say about it, and the four things every call has to establish.

blocks.html:
This is a meal delivery benefit that is already included in the consumer's Medicaid. Up to 3 meals a day, at no cost to them, delivered to their door, with no change to their coverage.

You are not selling it. You are not signing anyone up. You confirm four things and hand the consumer to a screener.

The four things:

  1. They still receive Medicaid
  2. Their borough
  3. Their ZIP code
  4. All of it again, as a double confirm

Then you get their okay and bring the screener on.

blocks.title: What you may say
blocks.html: Up to 3 meals a day · at no cost · included in your Medicaid · delivered to your doorstep · no change to your coverage · you're already approved. All of that is approved wording.

blocks.title: What you may never say
blocks.html: That it costs anything. That their coverage changes. A delivery date. A dollar amount. A specific menu. The screener handles all of that — and two of those are simply untrue.

blocks.question: What is this benefit?
choices: A meal delivery benefit already included in their Medicaid
A new insurance plan you're enrolling them in
blocks.explanation: Already included in their Medicaid. Nothing is being sold or changed.

lessons.title: The call is short — much shorter than you think

blocks.html: Across 3,263 real calls, a typical one runs about a minute and a half. When a consumer brushes you off and the agent doesn't come straight back, the median call is 27 seconds.
That is the whole reason the script says GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE after every rebuttal. It isn't a style note. You have seconds.

blocks.title: Consumers answer in two or three words
blocks.html: “Yes.” “No.” “What?” “Who's this?” That is normal on this campaign. Don't mistake a short answer for rudeness, and don't fill the silence with a speech.

blocks.question: A consumer says “not interested” four seconds into the call. What does the data say happens next?
choices: The consumer usually asks a question
It makes no difference to the outcome
Most agents rebut and recover the call
Most of these calls end within seconds
blocks.explanation: 97.5% of calls where “not interested” comes up never reach a transfer. The window is tiny.

blocks.html: New York City Medicaid recipients across the five boroughs. Many are older. Many are hard of hearing. Many speak English as a second language. A lot of them have had several calls like this already.
Expect to repeat yourself, and expect suspicion — the most common single reaction on these calls is some version of “What?”

blocks.title: Slow down rather than speed up
blocks.html: If someone can't hear you, talking faster loses the call. The verifications are short; say them clearly and wait.

blocks.question: A consumer asks you to repeat yourself twice in the first fifteen seconds. What's the right move?
choices: Transfer them to the screener early
blocks.explanation: Hard of hearing is normal here, not a brush-off.

lessons.title: What the screener does, and what you don't

blocks.html: The screener sets up the service. They cover delivery, menus, timing and anything specific. Your job ends when they're talking to the consumer.

So when a consumer asks “when do the meals come?” or “can I pick what I get?”, the honest and compliant answer is the same: the screener will go over that — and then straight back to your verification.

blocks.title: Guessing is how agents get in trouble
blocks.html: Promising a delivery date or a specific menu is a compliance failure even when you're trying to be helpful. You genuinely don't know, and the consumer remembers what you told them.

blocks.question: “When will my first delivery come?”
choices: “The screener will go over all of that with you — I just need to confirm…”
blocks.explanation: You don't know, and the script sends it to the screener.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hey, good morning, am I speaking with Maria?

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hey Maria, this is Nate, I'm with America's Health on a recorded line. We were just giving you a quick call today about the Medicaid meal service for you and your family. I just need to confirm you ARE still receiving Medicaid, correct?

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Okay perfect, and you're still in the Bronx, with the zip code 10457, correct?

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Okay LAST question here, JUST to double confirm, you ARE receiving Medicaid and you ARE still in the Bronx, correct?

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Perfect, that's everything I need. The screener is coming on the line now to help you set that up, once that's finished they'll have you on your way, okay?

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: (warm handoff naming the consumer, borough and ZIP)

blocks.html: Four verifications, a permission, a handoff. Under ninety seconds. That's the job.

blocks.question: How many separate times is Medicaid confirmed on a correct call?
choices: Twice — the first ask and the double confirm
blocks.explanation: The first ask, then again in the double confirm before the transfer.

questions.question: What is the meal benefit?
choices: A benefit already included in their Medicaid
A new plan you enrol them in

questions.question: How many meals a day may you mention?
questions.explanation: Up to 3 meals a day is approved wording.

questions.question: Which of these may you NOT say?
choices: There's no change to your coverage
questions.explanation: Delivery dates belong to the screener and you don't know them.

questions.question: A typical call on this campaign runs about…
questions.explanation: Around a minute and a half. Brush-off calls that aren't rebutted die at 27 seconds.

questions.question: What are the four things you confirm?
choices: Medicaid, borough, ZIP, then all of it again
Borough, ZIP, meals wanted, delivery day

questions.question: Who handles delivery and menu questions?
questions.explanation: The screener. Redirect and go back to verifying.

questions.question: A consumer answers “yes” in one word. That is…
choices: A reason to slow the pitch
questions.explanation: Two or three word answers are the norm here.

questions.question: Why does the script say “don't stop or pause”?
choices: Because brush-off calls end in seconds if you hesitate
questions.explanation: 27 seconds is the median when a brush-off goes unrebutted.
